newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: Former Papua New Guinea PM Wingti set to lose seat.
newsitem.headline: Former Papua New Guinea PM Wingti set to lose seat.

text.p: Former Papua New Guinea prime minister Paias Wingti on Tuesday faced defeat in national elections, which have been marked by a rejection of sitting parliamentarians.

Wingti, who served twice as prime minister in the late 1980s and early 1990s and had signalled his interest in a third term, was trailing a local Catholic priest who held a comfortable lead in a Western Highlands electorate with most votes counted, according to poll results.
Seventeen of the South Pacific country's 109 parliamentary seats have so far been decided in the two-week long elections which began 10 days ago, with eight falling to new candidates.
The election is seen as crucial to the future stability of the South Pacific nation, which experienced the worst crisis in its 21-year independent history after an army mutiny in April.

Faced with the revolt and violent civil protests, Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan was forced to step aside over plans to use British-led mercenaries to quash a nine-year secessionist uprising on Bougainville.
He resumed power three weeks ago in time for the elections, which began ten days ago.
Of the 17 seats declared, five have gone to independents, including the first woman to hold a seat in 10 years, Lady Carol Kidu, the Australian-born widow of the late chief justice Sir Buri Kidu.
Chan is expected to retain his seat in the province of New Ireland in the north of the country, but will face at least four challengers in parliament for the post of prime minister.
Governor of the national capital Port Moresby Bill Skate, who polled strongly to retain his seat, had indicated he will try for the post.

Deputy prime minisiter and finance mininster Chris Haiveta, who was criticised by an inquiry into the mercenary affair, has also said he will stand, as has former army commander and politician Ted Diro.
The country's first prime minister Sir Michael Somare, who led the country to independence from Australia in 1975, has also expressed interest in challenging Chan.
Up to three million citizens can vote and voting across the country will take up to two weeks to allow voters from remote villages to reach polling stations.

Election related violence aimed at disrupting polling has marred the election, mainly in the rugged highlands region, and voting officials said it appeared many election petitions would be lodged over alleged voting irregularities.
A new government is not expected to be formed until late July after a considerable amount of horse-trading amongst the new parliamentarians.
